With many of us goats staying inside these days, there is a wealth of old American cinema available for free on YouTube and various websites. Movies are in our blood, as Americans. His Woman (1931) with Gary Cooper -- this film focuses on the interpersonal relationships between a U.S. Navy ship captain in southeast Asia and a young woman (Claudette Colbert) he picks up in port. Accurate to the time, someone abandons a baby on the ship while it is at port. The undertone of American sailors --- portrayed as largely morally loss men --- having X rated fun in ports around the Philippines and Thailand is present. Claudette Colbert plays a young woman, a prostitute or "entertainer", who portrays herself as a well-to-do missionary's daughter with a few wardrobe changes. She's looking to travel back to New York, and wouldn't you know, the U.S. naval ship is headed there too! The feminine cunning is on full display in Claudette's performance. However, the audience grows to like this female character due to her complete transition to faux motherhood with the abandoned baby. Captain Gary Cooper is at his wits end, finding a caregiver for this abandoned on a ship full of men. Colbert's character is just the ticket and the two end up developing mutual admiration for each other. At one point in the film, the naval captain wants to abandon the baby in port, but is stopped from doing so by two black porters. The respect for life runs like an eddy through the story. Of course, this is an American movie and just like in our forefather's Shakespeare, American comedies tend to end in marriage. Cooper's character and Colbert's character are set to be married on shore in New York when Colbert's past comes spilling out. It's a tense moment -- will there be a redemption arc for Colbert's whore / Madonna mix?

Desire (1936) . Gary Cooper and Marlene Dietrich team up in this jewelry heist / comedy of errors piece. Cooper plays an ambitious motor engineer, straight from Detroit, designing highly successful carburetors in Paris. When's the last time the leading man was an engineer and not a businessman, financier, spy, military man, etc. in American cinema? But back in the 30s, mechanical engineers were rightfully lauded and we see that respect in the films from that time. Dietrich, in classic 1930s feminine form, is an untrustworthy femme fatale. Playing powerful men off of each other in Paris, she escapes with a 2.5 million franc pearl necklace. But she has car trouble and who is there to save her? Cooper, on his two week vacation in Europe! Dietrich portrays subtle sexuality better than any actress could nowadays, and her German accent is a delight. Cooper, with his Montana profile in every black and white shot, is starstruck by this woman. But he's no simp. He's happy to abandon her by the Spanish wayside when she gets mouthy and manages to track her down in Spain when she steals his car. The gender dynamic between the two characters is neither sheer sex nor lust. It is much more complex than that because this was the 1930s, when social nuance had meaning. This film shows off an impeccable wardrobe in Dietrich, as well as magic tricks (!) and snappy dialogue. Will the American mechanic and the European criminal end up together, destined for domestic bliss back in America? Or will they use and abuse each other like the best of them?
